content.title: About
content.content: Bay leaves are the leaves of the bay laurel (Laurus nobilis), an evergreen tree native to the Mediterranean. They have a spicy, slightly bitter aroma with notes of mint, pine, and clove. In cooking, dried leaves are usually used, added to soups, meat dishes, sauces, and marinades and removed before serving.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: In ancient Greece and Rome, wreaths of laurel branches were made for victors.
Dried leaves are more aromatic than fresh ones, and their aroma develops during long cooking.
The leaves stay tough even after cooking, which is why they are removed from the dish.
Indian bay leaf (tej patta) is a different plant with a flavor resembling cinnamon.
Cherry laurel and oleander have similar-looking leaves but are poisonous.

items.title: Contains essential oils
items.content: The aromatic compounds in bay leaf, such as cineole, give it its distinctive smell.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: The leaves contain polyphenols with antioxidant properties.

items.title: Adds flavor without extra salt
items.content: The aromatic leaf makes dishes richer without adding salt or calories.

items.title: Traditionally used for digestion
items.content: In folk practice, bay leaf tea is used for stomach discomfort, but there is little scientific evidence.

items.title: Contains small amounts of minerals
items.content: The leaves contain calcium, iron, and manganese, but the amounts in a dish are small.

items.title: Should not be eaten whole
items.content: The tough leaves are hard to chew and can get stuck in the throat or injure the intestines, so they should be removed from the dish.

items.title: Poisonous look-alikes
items.content: Cherry laurel and oleander leaves are poisonous; use only true bay laurel from a reliable source.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Allergic reactions and contact dermatitis are possible.

items.title: Essential oil
items.content: Bay essential oil should not be taken internally.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Add one or two dried leaves to soup, borscht, broth, braised meat, rice, sauces, and marinades at the start of cooking, and always remove them before serving. For a stronger aroma, lightly crack the leaf.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dried leaves in an airtight jar in a dry, dark place. The aroma fades over time, so use them within a year or two. Fresh leaves can be kept in the refrigerator or dried.
